summary.text: Taking \(p=3\) and \(r=2\), direct evaluation gives \(a(9)-a(3)=2343591352008=3^9\cdot119066776\), with the second factor not divisible by \(3\), so the difference has exact \(3\)-adic valuation \(9\) and is not divisible by the required \(3^{12}\). Thus the stronger modulus used in the accepted statement fails at this instance (while the difference is divisible by the originally stated \(3^9\)).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2,
\qquad
C(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k},
\]
so that the sequence under consideration is
\[
a(n)=5A(n)+14C(n-1).
\]

The universally quantified statement actually disproved in the accepted submission uses the modulus
\[
p^3\,p^r\,p^{2r}\,p^3=p^{3r+6}.
\]
We disprove that stronger statement by taking
\[
p=3,\qquad r=2.
\]
These parameters satisfy all its hypotheses: 3 is prime, \(3\geq 3\), and \(2\geq2\). The two sequence indices in the asserted congruence are
\[
p^r=3^2=9,\qquad p^{r-1}=3^1=3,
\]
and the modulus in the accepted formal statement becomes
\[
3^3\cdot3^2\cdot3^4\cdot3^3=3^{12}=531441.
\]
It remains to calculate \(a(9)\) and \(a(3)\).

First calculate \(a(3)=5A(3)+14C(2)\). The individual summands in \(A(3)\), for \(k=0,1,2,3\), are respectively
\[
\binom30^2\binom30^2=1,
\]
\[
\binom31^2\binom41^2=3^2\cdot4^2=144,
\]
\[
\binom32^2\binom52^2=3^2\cdot10^2=900,
\]
and
\[
\binom33^2\binom63^2=1^2\cdot20^2=400.
\]
Consequently
\[
A(3)=1+144+900+400=1445.
\]
Similarly, the three summands in \(C(2)\) are
\[
\binom20^2\binom20=1,
\qquad
\binom21^2\binom31=2^2\cdot3=12,
\qquad
\binom22^2\binom42=1^2\cdot6=6.
\]
Thus
\[
C(2)=1+12+6=19,
\]
and hence
\[
a(3)=5\cdot1445+14\cdot19=7225+266=7491.
\]

Next calculate \(a(9)=5A(9)+14C(8)\). For \(A(9)\), the ten values of
\(
\binom9k^2\binom{9+k}{k}^2
\)
for \(k=0,1,\ldots,9\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
k&\binom9k^2\binom{9+k}{k}^2\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&8100\\
2&3920400\\
3&341510400\\
4&8116208100\\
5&63631071504\\
6&176752976400\\
7&169612185600\\
8&47869064100\\
9&2363904400
\end{array}
\]
Adding these ten integers gives
\[
A(9)=468690849005.
\]

For \(C(8)\), the nine values of
\(
\binom8k^2\binom{8+k}{k}
\)
for \(k=0,1,\ldots,8\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
k&\binom8k^2\binom{8+k}{k}\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&576\\
2&35280\\
3&517440\\
4&2425500\\
5&4036032\\
6&2354352\\
7&411840\\
8&12870
\end{array}
\]
Their sum is
\[
C(8)=9793891.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
 &=5\cdot468690849005+14\cdot9793891\\
 &=2343454245025+137114474\\
 &=2343591359499.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore the relevant difference is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)-a(3)
 &=2343591359499-7491\\
 &=2343591352008\\
 &=3^9\cdot119066776.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining factor is not divisible by 3: indeed, its decimal digit sum is
\[
1+1+9+0+6+6+7+7+6=43,
\]
which is not divisible by 3. Equivalently, one may note the more precise congruence
\[
119066776\equiv16\pmod{27}.
\]
Thus the 3-adic valuation of \(a(9)-a(3)\) is exactly 9. In particular,
\[
3^{12}\nmid a(9)-a(3).
\]
Indeed, division modulo \(3^{12}\) gives the nonzero remainder
\[
a(9)-a(3)\equiv3^9\cdot16=314928\pmod{3^{12}}.
\]
Hence
\[
a(3^2)\not\equiv a(3^{2-1})\pmod{3^3\,3^2\,3^{2\cdot2}\,3^3}.
\]
This single admissible pair \((p,r)=(3,2)\) contradicts the universal assertion with modulus \(p^3p^rp^{2r}p^3=p^{3r+6}\), and therefore disproves the stronger statement appearing in the accepted submission.

There is an essential distinction between that statement and the canonical OEIS conjecture quoted in the question. The canonical modulus is only
\[
p^{3r+3}.
\]
At \((p,r)=(3,2)\), this is \(3^9\), not \(3^{12}\). The factorization above shows that
\[
3^9\mid a(9)-a(3),
\]
so in fact
\[
a(9)\equiv a(3)\pmod{3^9}.
\]
Accordingly, the accepted counterexample disproves the accidentally strengthened modulus \(p^{3r+6}\), but it does not disprove the canonical OEIS conjecture modulo \(p^{3r+3}\). A disproof of the canonical formulation cannot honestly be inferred from this accepted argument.
